opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, this is something I think about a lot. My general instinct is to give the model less scaffolding than you'd expect, but more context than you'd expect. People often confuse the two.

What I mean is that a lot of people, when they first start building with these models, write very rigid, step-by-step instructions. "First do X, then check Y, then output Z in this exact format." That made sense a couple of model generations ago, when you really had to hold the model's hand. But as models have gotten more capable, that kind of heavy scaffolding can actually box them in. You end up encoding your own assumptions about how the task should be solved, and if those assumptions are slightly wrong, or the situation is a bit different from what you anticipated, the model follows your recipe off a cliff instead of doing the sensible thing.

What I find works much better is to treat the model the way you'd treat a smart new hire. You wouldn't give a talented engineer a 40-step checklist on day one. You'd explain the goal, why it matters, what good looks like, what the constraints are, and maybe the pitfalls you've seen before. Then you trust them to figure out the how. So I spend a lot of my prompting effort on the "why" and the "what does success look like," and much less on dictating the procedure.

A useful test I come back to is: if I handed this prompt to a really sharp human expert with no other context, would they be able to do a great job? If not, it's usually because I've left out context that lives in my head, not because I haven't given enough instructions. And if the human would find it weirdly over-specified or patronizing, that's often a sign I'm over-scaffolding.

The other piece is tools and environment. A lot of what people try to do with prompt scaffolding is better done by giving the model good tools and letting it act in a loop. Instead of saying "think about whether the code compiles," just let it run the compiler. Instead of elaborate instructions on how to search, give it a good search tool with a clear description. Good tool design, clear names, sensible parameters, helpful error messages, often matters more than the system prompt itself.

That said, it isn't zero scaffolding. If there are hard constraints, like "never touch production," "this output gets parsed by a machine, so the format is strict," or "these are the things that went wrong last time," you should absolutely state them clearly. And for simpler or cheaper models, or for very high-volume, narrow tasks, a more structured workflow can still be the right call, because predictability matters more than flexibility there.

So my rough heuristic is: start simple, give rich context and a clear goal, watch what the model actually does, and only add structure where you see it consistently going wrong. Add scaffolding in response to observed failures, not anticipated ones. And every time a new model comes out, go back and see what you can delete, because often the thing that was necessary six months ago is now just getting in the way.

r001.rationale: The response says to give a talented engineer context, goals, constraints, and success criteria, while giving less scaffolding. It does not clearly say that highly capable human experts still use scaffolding.

r002.rationale: It proposes checking whether a sharp human expert with no other context could do a great job, and using that to identify what the prompt needs.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, this is something I've changed my mind on a lot over the past couple of years. My instinct early on, coming from robotics and more traditional engineering, was to be very prescriptive: break the task into steps, give the model a rigid flow, check its work at every stage. And that worked for a while, but what we kept seeing is that every piece of scaffolding you add is also a ceiling. You're baking in your own assumptions about how the problem should be solved, and the model is often better at the problem than you are at anticipating it.

So the heuristic I've landed on is something like: give the model the goal and the context, give it good tools, and get out of the way. Describe what success looks like, what the constraints are, what it has access to, and then trust it to figure out the path. The place where I still spend a lot of effort is on the tools and the environment rather than the instructions. If the model can run tests, read the actual files, check its own output, it will self-correct in ways that no amount of prompting could substitute for. Feedback loops beat instructions.

The other thing I'd say is that the right amount of scaffolding is a moving target. Scaffolding is basically a patch for model limitations, and the limitations keep shrinking. We've had internal cases where a carefully engineered multi-step pipeline got beaten by just handing the whole task to a newer model with a one-paragraph prompt. So I try to build things in a way where the scaffolding is easy to remove. If you've designed your system so the model can only do one narrow thing, you don't get to benefit when the next model comes out.

Where I do still think structure matters is in making the task legible: making sure the model knows what's expected, what the acceptance criteria are, when it should stop and ask versus proceed. That's less about controlling how it works and more about communicating clearly, the same way you'd onboard a new engineer. You wouldn't hand them a flowchart. You'd tell them what you're trying to accomplish and make sure they could get to the information they need.

r001.rationale: The response compares task guidance to onboarding a new engineer, but does not say that highly capable human experts still use scaffolding.

r002.rationale: The response uses a human-onboarding analogy, but does not propose calibrating AI instructions based on how much instruction a human would need for the same task.

astra-6.text:
I think of it as a spectrum. At one end, you specify every step: do this, then do that, then check the result. At the other end, you give the model a goal and let it figure out how to get there.

I usually start with the simplest version: give it a clear goal, the context it needs, and a way to tell whether it succeeded. Then see where it gets stuck. If it consistently makes a particular mistake, add structure there. You might need a better tool, an example, or an explicit check—not necessarily a much longer prompt.

The tradeoff is that scaffolding can improve reliability, but it also encodes your assumptions about how the task should be solved. If you prescribe every step, you can prevent the model from finding a better approach. So I’d be very explicit about the outcome and the constraints, and give it as much freedom over the method as it can handle reliably.

r001.rationale: The response discusses scaffolding for AI models but does not say that highly capable human experts also use scaffolding.

r002.rationale: It recommends starting with a goal and adding structure where the model struggles, but does not calibrate instructions by considering what a human would need for the same task.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of it as a tradeoff between giving the model enough context to succeed and constraining it so much that it can’t find a better approach. You want to be clear about the goal, the constraints, and how it can tell whether it’s done. But you don’t necessarily want to prescribe every step.

My approach is to start with the simplest setup and look at where it fails. Is it missing information? Does it need a tool? Does it misunderstand what a good result looks like? Then add scaffolding that addresses that specific failure, rather than trying to anticipate everything up front.

And as the models improve, you should revisit those decisions. A workflow that helped an earlier model might become unnecessary, or even get in the way. So I’d treat the scaffolding as something you’re continually testing, rather than a permanent part of the system.

r001.rationale: The response discusses scaffolding for AI models but does not say that highly capable human experts also use scaffolding.

r002.rationale: It recommends adjusting scaffolding based on where the model fails, but does not calibrate instructions by considering how much help a human would need for the same task.
